items.stem: Concrete is strong in compression but weak in tension. Why is steel reinforcement placed in the bottom of a simply supported beam?

options.text: Because the bottom fibres are in tension under downward load and steel carries that tension
options.rationale: Correct: reinforcement is placed where tension develops.

options.text: Because the bottom is colder and steel prefers cold
options.rationale: Temperature is not the reason for reinforcement placement.

options.text: Because steel is cheaper at the bottom
options.rationale: Cost does not determine structural placement.

options.text: Because the top of the beam carries no load
options.rationale: The top is in compression; reinforcement location follows tension.

items.explanation: Correct: reinforcement is placed where tension develops.

items.stem: Which TWO are examples of lateral load-resisting systems? (Select TWO.)

options.rationale: Correct: shear walls resist lateral loads.
Correct: braced frames resist lateral loads.
Floor joists carry gravity loads, not primarily lateral loads.

options.text: A spread footing under a column
options.rationale: A footing transfers load to the ground; it is not a lateral system.

items.stem: Following the load path for a typical floor, in what order does gravity load travel to the ground?

options.text: Slab to beams to columns to foundations to soil
options.rationale: Correct: this is the typical downward gravity load path.

options.text: Soil to foundations to slab to occupants
options.rationale: That reverses the actual direction of load flow.

options.text: Columns to slab to wind to roof
options.rationale: This mixes unrelated elements and directions.

options.text: Foundations to beams to slab to columns
options.rationale: This is not a coherent load path order.

items.explanation: Correct: this is the typical downward gravity load path.
